metadata.title: Profiles of occupational well-being among Chinese teachers: Associations with basic psychological needs satisfaction and teaching quality

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the China TALIS 2018 teacher dataset, restricted to middle school teachers (Grades 7–9) in Shanghai. The manuscript reports the TALIS sampling as nationally representative at the TALIS level, but it does not specify whether TALIS teacher sampling weights were applied in the analyses. Because the core analyses are person-centered latent profile analysis and subsequent profile comparisons (implemented in MPlus), the paper does not report any complex survey weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures. Therefore, weighting cannot be confirmed from the provided text; readers should treat the results as conditional on the Shanghai analytic sample and the reported model-based estimates rather than as explicitly population-weighted TALIS inferences.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The study does not use cognitive achievement plausible values (PVs); outcomes are teacher job satisfaction, stress, basic psychological needs satisfaction, and teaching quality measured via Likert-type questionnaire scales and latent constructs. For missing data, the authors state that missingness was handled using full information maximum likelihood (FIML) under a missing completely at random assumption; in this schema, FIML is mapped to multiple_imputation. Because the paper does not describe PV-specific procedures, PV handling is not applicable by design for these non-achievement outcomes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the China TALIS 2018 dataset and restricted the analytic sample to middle school teachers (Grades 7–9) from Shanghai, China. The paper reports that missing data at the variable level ranged from 1.1% to 18.6% and that missingness was assessed as missing completely at random (Little & Rubin; normed chi-square χ2/df = 1.55), after which FIML was used rather than listwise deletion. No other exclusions (e.g., by subject taught or employment status) are described for the main latent profile estimation sample.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Latent profile analysis fit: 4-profile solution selected (AIC/BIC/SSA-BIC decreased; 5–8 profiles excluded due to <5% class size; 4-profile solution had significant LMR and BLRT p-values and higher entropy). Profile sizes: Profile 1 highly satisfied n=507 (12.8%), Profile 2 balanced n=2726 (69.0%), Profile 3 highly unsatisfied n=399 (10.1%), Profile 4 highly stressed n=320 (8.1%). Additional analysis (Teaching quality differences across occupational well-being profiles): Chi-squared tests for distal outcomes across 4 profiles: clarity of instruction χ2(3)=132.602, p<.001; cognitive activation χ2(3)=59.424, p<.001; classroom management χ2(3)=117.624, p<.001. Profile means (Table 5): Clarity—Profile 1 14.71, Profile 2 13.50, Profile 3 13.61, Profile 4 13.45; Cognitive activation—Profile 1 11.84, Profile 2 10.58, Profile 3 10.67, Profile 4 11.23; Classroom management—Profile 1 8.77, Profile 2 9.18, Profile 3 8.93, Profile 4 6.78.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 China (Shanghai), Grades 7–9 teacher survey the study leveraged Autonomy (basic needs), Competence (basic needs), Relatedness (basic needs), Gender, and First choice of career to characterize occupational well-being profile membership, finding that higher autonomy, competence, and relatedness were associated with greater likelihood of belonging to the highly satisfied profile, while gender and career-choice variables also differentiated profile membership. This indicates that teacher well-being is meaningfully segmented into distinct subgroups and that basic psychological needs and demographic/career factors can guide targeted support rather than one-size-fits-all interventions.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzed TALIS 2018 China teacher data restricted to Shanghai middle school teachers (Grades 7–9), with a total analytic sample of 3,976 teachers. The authors used a person-centered approach (latent profile analysis) to identify four occupational well-being profiles—highly satisfied (n=507), balanced (n=2,726), highly unsatisfied (n=399), and highly stressed (n=320)—and then examined how basic psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy, competence, relatedness) and demographics related to profile membership. They reported significant profile differences in teaching quality: clarity of instruction (χ2(3)=132.602, p<.001), cognitive activation (χ2(3)=59.424, p<.001), and classroom management (χ2(3)=117.624, p<.001), with highly satisfied teachers highest on clarity and cognitive activation and highly stressed teachers lowest on classroom management. Missing data were handled via FIML under a missing-completely-at-random assumption, but the paper does not report PV handling or explicit TALIS sampling weights, and the cross-sectional design prevents causal inference.
